content: 1. Consent must be obtained before proceeding with any medical intervention or procedure. This ensures that the client is fully informed and agrees to the proposed course of action. 2. Depending on the chosen contraceptive method, additional examinations and tests may be required to assess the client’s eligibility for the method and to determine the most appropriate time to initiate it. These tests are also conducted to ensure the safety of the method for the client. 3. The examinations and tests recommended for each type of contraceptive are generally designed for individuals presumed to be healthy. Clients with known medical conditions or special circumstances may require further evaluations or tests to ensure safety and suitability. 4. The feasibility of conducting specific tests should also be considered. For instance, if a healthcare facility lacks the resources to perform a hemoglobin test, the absence of this test should not prevent the client from accessing contraceptive methods. 5. When providing a contraceptive method, it is essential to explain to the client how the method works, how to use it, when to start, and how to identify and manage potential side effects. For methods like subcutaneous depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA-SC), guided training may be necessary for self-administration. 6. Long-acting and permanent contraceptive methods require a procedural intervention, which should be performed in a clinical setting following established guidelines. 7. Certain methods, such as intrauterine devices (IUDs) and implants, may necessitate in-clinic observation and a rest period after insertion to monitor for immediate complications. 8. Dual protection should be discussed with clients to emphasize the importance of preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs), reproductive tract infections, and unintended pregnancies. If a backup method is required, clients should use condoms or abstain from sexual activity for the recommended duration. 9. Clients should be encouraged to ask questions and seek clarification about their chosen method. For self-administered methods, ensure the client has received adequate training and knows they can return to the facility at any time for assistance. 10. Follow-up requirements vary depending on the contraceptive method. While some methods require regular follow-up visits, clients should always be encouraged to return if they experience side effects, complications, or wish to change methods. 11. If follow-up is required, schedule a visit and explain its importance. Confirm the client’s contact information if they consent to being contacted for follow-up purposes. 12. Even if routine follow-up is not necessary, clients should be informed that they are welcome to return at any time to address side effects, complications, or concerns about pregnancy or STI risks. 13. In cases where a referral is needed, such as when a facility cannot provide a specific method or service, the client should be directed to an appropriate referral facility. Emergency referrals should bypass standard steps to ensure immediate care. 14. Stabilize clients requiring emergency referrals and provide pre-referral treatment as needed. Once stable, arrange for immediate transport to the referral facility. 15. Discuss referral location options with the client and their family, including transportation logistics, the services available at the referral facility, and follow-up plans upon return. 16. Contact the referral facility to confirm their ability to accommodate the client and provide the necessary services. If the facility cannot accommodate the client, identify an alternative facility. 17. Provide the referral facility with all relevant clinical, sociodemographic, and identification information about the client. This can be done digitally if systems are in place. 18. For adolescents requiring referrals, ensure they are accompanied by a responsible adult to the referral facility. 19. Aggregate client-level data into validated reports for use in monitoring progress, making decisions, and submitting reports to higher levels of the health system. Data quality should be reviewed for accuracy, validity, and completeness. 20. Feedback mechanisms should be in place to address any issues with submitted data, allowing for corrections and resubmission if necessary. 21. Digital systems should be adapted to local contexts, with workflows customized to reflect the specific needs and practices of the healthcare facility. This includes conducting interviews and shadowing healthcare workers to ensure the system aligns with real-world requirements. 22. Core data elements should be identified and included in the system to support service delivery, decision-making, and performance monitoring. Data collection should not hinder client access to contraceptive methods or compromise clinical care.
